[[File:Cantor set in seven iterations.svg|alt=Seven iterations of the construction of the Cantor ternary set, an example of a fractal string.|thumb|309x309px|Seven iterations of the construction of the [[Cantor ternary set]], an example of a fractal string.]]
An ordinary '''fractal string''' <math> \Omega </math> is a bounded, open subset of the [[real number line]]. Such a subset can be written as an at-most-[[countable set|countable]] union of connected [[open interval]]s with associated lengths <math> \mathcal{L}=\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\ldots\} </math> written in non-increasing order; we also refer to <math>\mathcal{L}</math> as a '''fractal string'''. For example, <math> \mathcal{L}=\left\{ \frac 1 3, \frac 1 9, \frac 1 9,\ldots\right\} </math> is a fractal string corresponding to the [[Cantor set]]. A fractal string is the analogue of a one-dimensional "fractal drum," and typically the set <math>\Omega</math> has a boundary <math>\partial\Omega</math> which corresponds to a fractal such as the Cantor set. The heuristic idea of a fractal string is to study a (one-dimensional) fractal using the "space around the fractal." It turns out that the sequence of lengths <math>\mathcal{L}</math> of the set itself is "intrinsic," in the sense that the fractal string <math>\mathcal{L}</math> itself (independent of a specific geometric realization of these lengths as corresponding to a choice of set <math>\Omega</math>) contains information about the fractal to which it corresponds.<ref name="one" />

For each fractal string <math> \mathcal{L} </math>, we can associate to <math> \mathcal{L} </math> a '''geometric zeta function''' <math> \zeta_{\mathcal{L}} </math>: the [[Dirichlet series]] <math> \zeta_{\mathcal{L}} (s)=\sum_{j \in \mathbb{J}} \ell_j^{s} </math>. Informally, the geometric zeta function carries geometric information about the underlying fractal, particularly in the location of its [[Zeros and poles|poles]] and the [[Residue (complex analysis)|residues]] of the zeta function at these poles. These poles of (the [[analytic continuation]] of) the geometric zeta function <math> \zeta_{\mathcal{L}} (s) </math> are then called '''complex dimensions''' of the fractal string <math> \mathcal{L} </math>, and these complex dimensions appear in formulae which describe the geometry of the fractal.<ref name="one" />

For fractal strings associated with sets like Cantor sets, formed from deleted intervals that are [[rational number|rational]] powers of a fundamental length, the complex dimensions appear in an arithmetic progression parallel to the imaginary axis, and are called '''lattice''' fractal strings (For example, the complex dimensions of the Cantor set are <math> s=\frac{\log 2 + 2 \pi i k}{\log 3} </math>, which are an arithmetic progression in the direction of the imaginary axis). Otherwise, they are called '''non-lattice'''. In fact, an ordinary fractal string is Minkowski measurable if and only if it is non-lattice.

A '''generalized fractal string''' <math>\eta</math> is defined to be a local positive or complex measure on <math>(0, +\infty)</math> such that <math>|\eta|(0, x_0) = 0</math> for some <math>x_0 > 0</math>, where the positive measure <math>|\eta|</math> is the [[total variation]] measure associated to <math>\eta</math>. These generalized fractal strings allow for lengths to be given non-integer multiplicities (among other possibilities), and each ordinary fractal string can be associated with a measure that makes it into a generalized fractal string.

== Ordinary fractal strings ==

An ordinary [[fractal]] string <math> \Omega </math> is a bounded, open subset of the real number line. Any such subset can be written as an at-most-[[countable set|countable]] union of connected [[open interval]]s with associated lengths <math> \mathcal{L}=\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\ldots\} </math> written in non-increasing order. We allow <math> \Omega </math> to consist of finitely many open intervals, in which case <math> \mathcal{L} </math> consists of finitely many lengths. We refer to <math> \mathcal{L} </math> as a ''fractal string''.

===Example===
The [[Cantor ternary set|middle third's Cantor set]] is constructed by removing the middle third from the unit interval <math> (0,1) </math>, then removing the middle thirds of the subsequent intervals, ''ad infinitum''. The deleted intervals <math> \Omega=\left\{ \left(\frac 1 3, \frac 2 3 \right), \left( \frac 1 9, \frac 2 9 \right), \left( \frac 7 9, \frac 8 9 \right),\ldots\right\} </math> have corresponding lengths <math> \mathcal{L}=\left\{ \frac 1 3, \frac 1 9, \frac 1 9,\ldots\right\} </math>. Inductively, we can show that there are <math> 2^{n-1} </math> intervals corresponding to each length of <math> 3^{-n}</math>. Thus, we say that the ''multiplicity'' of the length <math> 3^{-n} </math> is <math> 2^{n-1}</math>. The fractal string of the Cantor set is called the ''Cantor string''.<ref name="one" />

===Heuristic===

The geometric information of the Cantor set in the example above is contained in the ordinary fractal string <math> \mathcal{L} </math>. From this information, we can compute the [[box-counting dimension]] of the Cantor set. This notion of [[fractal dimension]] can be generalized to that of [[complex dimension]], which may be used to deduce geometrical information regarding the local oscillations in the geometry of the fractal. For example, the complex dimensions of a fractal string (such as the Cantor string) may be used to write an explicit tube formula for the volume of an [[Epsilon-neighborhood|<math>\varepsilon</math>-neighborhood]] of the fractal string, and the presence of non-real complex dimensions corresponds to oscillatory terms in this expansion.<ref name="one" />

==The geometric zeta function==
If <math> \sum_{j \in \mathbb{J}} {\ell_j}< \infty, </math> we say that <math> \Omega </math> has a geometric realization in <math> \mathbb{R},</math> <math> \Omega=\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty I_i </math>, where the <math>I_i </math> are intervals in <math>\mathbb{R} </math>, of all the lengths <math> \{ \ell_j \}_{j \in \mathbb{J}} </math>, taken with multiplicity.<ref name="one" />

For each fractal string <math> \mathcal{L} </math>, we can associate to <math> \mathcal{L} </math> a geometric zeta function <math> \zeta_{\mathcal{L}} </math> defined as the Dirichlet series <math> \zeta_{\mathcal{L}} (s)=\sum_{j \in \mathbb{J}} \ell_j^{s} </math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Herichi|first1=Hafedh|last2=Lapidus|first2=Michel L.|date=2012-09-01|title=Riemann zeros and phase transitions via the spectral operator on fractal strings|url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012JPhA...45K4005H|journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General|volume=45|issue=37|article-number=374005|arxiv=1203.4828|doi=10.1088/1751-8113/45/37/374005|bibcode=2012JPhA...45K4005H|s2cid=55352853|issn=0305-4470}}</ref> Poles of the geometric zeta function <math> \zeta_{\mathcal{L}} (s) </math> are called complex dimensions of the fractal string <math> \mathcal{L} </math>. The general philosophy of the theory of complex dimensions for fractal strings is that complex dimensions describe the intrinsic oscillation in the geometry, spectra and dynamics{{Weasel inline|date=December 2021}} of the fractal string <math> \mathcal{L} </math>.<ref name="one" />

The [[abscissa of convergence]] of <math> \zeta_{\mathcal{L}}(s) </math> is defined as <math> \sigma=\inf \left\{ \alpha \in \mathbb{R} : \sum_{j=1}^\infty \ell_j^\alpha < \infty \right\} </math>.<ref name=":0" />

For a fractal string <math> \mathcal{L} </math> with infinitely many nonzero lengths, the abscissa of convergence <math> \sigma </math> coincides with the [[Minkowski dimension]] of the boundary of the string, <math> \partial \Omega </math>.<ref name=":0" /> For our example, the boundary Cantor string is the Cantor set itself. So the abscissa of convergence of the geometric zeta function <math> \zeta_{\mathcal{L}}(s)  </math> is the Minkowski dimension of the Cantor set, which is <math> \frac{\log 2}{\log 3} </math>.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Falconer |first=K. J. |title=Fractal geometry: mathematical foundations and applications |date=2003 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=0-470-87135-0 |edition=2nd |location=Chichester |oclc=53970546}}</ref>

==Complex dimensions==

For a fractal string <math> \mathcal{L} </math>, composed of an infinite sequence of lengths, the ''complex dimensions'' of the fractal string are the poles of the analytic continuation of the geometric zeta function associated with the fractal string. (When the analytic continuation of a geometric zeta function is not defined to all of the complex plane, we take a subset of the complex plane called the "window", and look for the "visible" complex dimensions that exist within that window.<ref name=one/>)<ref name=":0" />

===Example===

Continuing with the example of the fractal string associated to the middle thirds Cantor set, we compute <math> \zeta_{\mathbb{C}}(s)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2^{n-1}}{3^{ns}} =\frac{\frac{1}{3^s}}{1-\frac{2}{3^s}} = \frac{1}{3^s - 2} </math>.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite conference |last=Radunović |first=Goran |date=28 June 2019 |title=An overview of the theory of complex dimensions and fractal zeta functions |url=https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~mresman/Dubrovnik_konf_06.19.pdf |conference=Dubrovnik IX - Topology & Dynamical Systems 2019}}</ref> We compute the [[abscissa of convergence]] to be the value of <math> s </math> satisfying <math> 3^s=2 </math>, so that <math> s=\log_3 2=\frac{\log 2}{\log 3} </math> is the [[Minkowski dimension]] of the Cantor set.<ref name=":2" /> For complex <math> s </math>, <math> \zeta_{\mathbb{C}}(s) </math> has [[pole (complex analysis)|poles]] at the infinitely many solutions of <math> 3^s=2 </math>, which, for this example, occur at <math> s=\frac{\log 2 + 2 \pi i k}{\log 3} </math>, for all integers <math> k </math>. This collection of points is called the set of complex dimensions of the middle thirds Cantor set.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

==Applications==
Ordinary and generalized fractal strings may be used to study the geometry of a (one-dimensional) fractal, as well as to relate the geometry of the object to its spectrum. For example, the geometric zeta function associated to a fractal string may be used to write an explicit tube formula for the volume of a neighborhood of the fractal.<ref name="one" /> Regarding the connection between geometry and spectra, the ''spectral zeta function'' of a fractal string, which is the geometric zeta function times the [[Riemann zeta function]], may be used to write explicit formulae which describe spectral counting functions.<ref name="one" />

The framework of fractal strings also serves to unify aspects of fractal and arithmetic geometry. For example, a general explicit formula for counting the (reciprocal) lengths of a fractal string may be used to prove [[Riemann's explicit formula]] when using a suitable generalized fractal string which is supported on the prime powers with multiplicities of each given by the logarithm of the prime base of the power.<ref name="one" />

For fractal strings associated with sets like Cantor sets, formed from deleted intervals that are [[rational number|rational]] powers of a fundamental length, the complex dimensions appear in a regular, arithmetic progression parallel to the imaginary axis, and are called ''lattice'' fractal strings. Sets that do not have this property are called ''non-lattice''. There is a dichotomy in the theory of measures of such objects: an ordinary fractal string is Minkowski measurable if and only if it is non-lattice.<ref name="one" />

The existence of non-real complex dimensions with positive real part has been proposed by Michel Lapidus and Machiel van Frankenhuijsen to be the signature feature of fractal objects.<ref name="one">M. L. Lapidus, M. van Frankenhuijsen, [https://www.springer.com/gb/book/9781461421757 Fractal Geometry, Complex Dimensions and Zeta Functions: Geometry and Spectra of Fractal Strings], Monographs in Mathematics, Springer, New York, Second revised and enlarged edition, 2012. {{doi|10.1007/978-1-4614-2176-4}}</ref> Formally, they propose to define "fractality" as the presence of at least one nonreal complex dimension with positive real part.<ref name="one" /> This new definition of fractality solves some old problems in fractal geometry. For example, according to the proposed definition of fractality in the sense of [[Benoit Mandelbrot|Mandelbrot]], [[Cantor function|Cantor's devil's staircase]] is not fractal because its Hausdorff and topological dimensions coincide.<ref name="one" /> However, the Cantor staircase function possesses many features which ought to be considered fractal such as self-similarity, and in this new sense of fractality the Cantor staircase function is considered fractal since it has non-real complex dimensions.<ref name="one" />

==Generalized fractal strings==
A generalized fractal string <math>\eta</math> is defined to be a local positive or local complex measure on <math>(0, +\infty)</math> such that <math>|\eta|(0, x_0) = 0</math> for some <math>x_0 > 0</math>, where the positive measure <math>|\eta|</math> is the [[total variation]] measure associated to <math>\eta</math>.<ref name="one" /><ref name=":0" /> A generalized fractal string allows for a fractal string to have a given set of lengths with non-integer multiplicities, or for a fractal string to have a continuum of lengths instead of discrete. By convention, a generalized fractal string is supported on reciprocal lengths as opposed to an ordinary fractal string which is a multiset of (decreasing or non-increasing) lengths. In light of this, the condition that the measure has "no mass near zero," or more precisely that there exists a positive number <math>x_0 > 0</math> such that the interval <math>(0,x_0)</math> has measure zero with respect to <math>|\eta|</math>, may be seen as an analogue of the boundedness of the ordinary fractal string.

For example, if <math>\mathcal{L} = \{l_j\}_{j=1}^{\infty}</math> is an ordinary fractal string with multiplicities <math>w_j</math>, then the measure <math>\eta_{\mathcal{L}} := \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} w_j\delta_{l_j^{-1}}</math> associated to <math>\mathcal{L}</math> (where <math>\delta_{\{x\}}</math> refers to the [[Dirac delta measure]] concentrated at the point <math>x</math>) is an example of a generalized fractal string.<ref name=":0" /> Note that the delta functions are supported on the singleton sets <math>\{\ell_j^{-1}\}</math> corresponding to the reciprocals of the lengths of the ordinary fractal string <math>\mathcal{L}</math>. If the multiplicities <math>w_j</math> are not positive integers, then <math>\eta_\mathcal{L}</math> is a generalized fractal string which cannot be realized as an ordinary fractal string. A concrete example of such a generalized fractal string would be the ''generalized Cantor string'' <math>\eta_{CS} := \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} b^j \delta_{a^j}</math> for <math>1 < b < a</math>.<ref name=":0" />

If <math>\eta</math> is a generalized fractal string, then its ''dimension'' is defined as <math display="block">D_{\eta} := \inf(\sigma\in\mathbb{R}: \int_0^{\infty} x^{-\sigma}|\eta|(dx) < \infty),</math>its ''counting function'' as

<math display="block">N_{\eta}(x) := \int_0^x \eta(dx) = \eta(0, x) +\frac12\eta(\{x\})</math>and its ''geometric zeta function'' (its [[Mellin transform]]) as

<math display="block">\zeta_{\eta}(s) := \int_0^{\infty} x^{-s}\eta(dx).</math><ref name=":0" /> (Note that the counting function is normalized at jump discontinuities to be half of the value at any singletons which have nonzero measure.)
